title: Excellence
hookLine: doing a job well is a form of love
tomorrow: who carries the other corners when the work gets heavy?

lines: PERFECT ROWS, OR A WARM SMILE?
cards: Two coworkers set up the same bakery case. One redoes the display until every row is perfect, and the line waits. The other rushes it, smiles at every customer, and leaves crumbs on the glass.
Which one did the job well? Customers would probably split. Catholic tradition has two strong answers, and they pull against each other in a useful way.

teach.b: The first voice says the craft matters. In the parable of the talents, the master doesn't praise good intentions.
He praises servants who actually traded and doubled what they were given: "Well done, good and faithful servant."

teach.h: HE HATH DONE ALL THINGS WELL.
teach.b: And when the crowd in Mark watches Jesus heal a deaf man, their verdict is about the work itself: "He hath done all things well." On this view, sloppy work isn't humble.
It's careless with the people who'll use it, and a shoddy thing is a poor gift to God.

teach.h: THE LOVE VOICE: THE LITTLE WAY.
teach.b: The second voice says love comes first. Paul writes that if he gave away everything he owned to feed the poor and had not charity, it would profit him nothing.

Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called her path the little way: small, hidden things done for love, where nobody is grading. On this view, chasing perfect can turn into pride, and God looks at the heart before the finish.
Both voices agree on one thing: the work is for someone.
The craft voice says love shows up in the details. The love voice says details without love are empty.

how: Catholics often look to Saint Joseph the worker and to Thérèse's little way when they talk about ordinary work done carefully and for love.

o: doing a job well as a way of loving people
a top grade given for flawless work
being ranked first among everyone at work

p: the master, to the faithful servant

s: in the parable, the master praises the servants' good intentions
he praises servants who traded and doubled what they were given.
Thérèse of Lisieux called her path the little way
small, hidden things done for love.
in Mark, the crowd says he hath done all things well
their verdict after he heals a deaf man.

games.q: one teammate redoes the group slides until midnight; another says good enough, it's one grade. what's the best case each could make?
o: one: careful work loves the people who use it. the other: perfect can turn into pride.
the midnight teammate is right; anything short of perfect is sloppy.
good enough is right; effort doesn't really matter to God.
games.why: the craft voice and the love voice are both Catholic, and each has a real case. they meet in the person the work is for.

practice: Take a pen and write down one piece of your work from this week that went out a little rough: an email, a shift, an assignment, a meal. Under it, write one small thing that would make it better for the person who receives it.

wordCard.voice: Excellence. A job done well, as a form of love for whoever it's for.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 25:21: well done, good servant.

carryVoice: Keep this one: well done, the small details as love made visible. Until tomorrow, then.
